title: Sarney-era reprivatizations (BNDESPar, Mafersa, Radiobras)
what: Under a Nov 1985 decree (Decreto 91.991), BNDESPar re-sold firms it had taken over for debts. BNDESPar counts 13 companies from June 1987 to Dec 1989. BNDES's own history counts 38 firms in the 1980s. The list of the 38 was not obtained. Radiobras stations were also transferred or closed from 1988.
who_got: Buyers and prices per firm were not found. Mafersa (rail equipment) was sold on 11 Nov 1991 to Refer. Refer sold 65% of it for R$1,000 in 1995. How Refer was financed was not found.
terms: Mafersa sold at Cr$143.50 per share against a minimum of Cr$54.95 (161% above). No overall valuation of the 1980s sales was found.
mechanism: Decreto 91.991/1985, then Decreto 95.886 of 29 Mar 1988 (Programa Federal de Desestatizacao). The 1988 decree revoked Decretos 91.991/1985 and 93.606/1986. Lei 8.031/1990 replaced it. The 1988 decree is known only from a search summary.

after: Mafersa ended in bankruptcy. In broadcasting, 23 of 37 Radiobras stations were transferred or closed, and 1,028 radio and TV licences were granted in the period.
counter_view: BNDES describes these sales as an orderly sale of firms acquired through rescue (BNDESPar paper). The 1988 decree gave two aims: shift activity to the private sector and cut the public deficit. The older note claim that the aim was 'not to raise money' is not supported by the decree summary.

title: National Privatization Programme (Lei 8.031/1990) and the 'moedas podres'
government: Collor; expanded under Itamar Franco and Cardoso (Lei 9.491/1997)
what: Legal framework for selling or conceding federal firms, run by BNDES. Bidders could pay with 'moedas de privatizacao': federal debt securities accepted at face value in auctions.
who_got: Bidders in the federal sales. Biondi (critical) says BNDES itself sold the 'moedas' to bidders, up to 12 years to pay, at privileged interest. IPEA also records BNDES selling securitized credits over 12 years at full monetary correction plus 6% a year.
terms: IPEA to mid-1993: about US$17 bn was expected; US$5.36 bn was raised at face value. Average premium (agio) 13.7%. Paid in: privatization certificates 24.2%; securitized Union debt 29.6% (83.4% of that was overdue Siderbras debts); Siderbras debentures 17.5%; FND 11.5%; TDA 8.3%; CEF letters 5.3%. Siderbras sales brought US$6.33 bn in 1991-93 against US$7 bn expected, 65% from steel; cash was about 3% of the Siderbras sales.
mechanism: Lei 8.031 (April 1990, 12 Apr by URL pattern, not opened); Lei 9.491 (9 Sep 1997 per a search result) set up the Conselho Nacional de Desestatizacao.
who_paid: The Treasury (discount on securities) and BNDES (credit to buyers). Steel workers paid in jobs (see the Siderbras case).
after: Cash grew over time: BCB 1996 shows cash rising from 36.4% of payments earlier to about 75% in 1996. BNDES says 'moedas' were heavily used in 1990-92, with more cash per deal in 1993-94 but 'not less important'. Sector agencies came later: Anatel was created by Lei 9.472 of 16 Jul 1997. ANEEL, ANP, ANTT and ANTAQ dates were not checked.
counter_view: BNDES presents 'moedas' as part of fiscal adjustment, cutting federal debt. The BCB 1996 report shows cash rising to about 75% of payments. Biondi's own table lists 'moedas' per company (Cosipa 99.6%, CSN 96%, Usiminas and others 100%), which conflicts with Garcia/Schmidt's Usiminas cash share of 2.6%. One search result says the 'moedas' traded at under half of face value; another says they were taken at face value (unreconciled).

title: BNDES loans to privatization buyers
government: Collor to Cardoso; audit in Lula's first year
what: BNDES was seller, adviser and lender in the sales. It financed bidders, mainly in electricity. The TCU audit found limits broken. A single all-sector total of buyer financing was not found.
who_got: Electricity buyers. AES owed BNDES US$1.2 bn. 12 distributors were financed by BNDES; 8 had not settled their debts by 2003. Early phase: BNDES sold securitized credits over 12 years at full monetary correction plus 6% a year (IPEA).
terms: Distributors yielded R$27 bn in sales but consumed R$22 bn of BNDES money; 14 of 22 firms got R$7 bn (TCU audit as reported). 20 distributors and 4 generators were sold for US$30 bn in 1995-2003.

who_paid: Taxpayers through the Treasury that funds BNDES. BNDES net worth fell from R$13 bn to R$10 bn between 2002 and mid-2003, but the cause is not isolated to these loans.
after: The 2003 AES deal gave BNDES 50% minus one share of Brasiliana and cut the debt to US$510 million. A R$3 bn capitalization line found no taker. TCU also audited the matter in a journal discussion.

title: PROER: credit for buyers of failing private banks

title: PROES and the sale of state banks
what: The Union took over state banks' debts and turned them into state debts to the Union over 30 years. It issued R$61.448 bn of bonds to sanitize state banks: SP R$36.1265 bn (23/24 Dec 1997), PR R$5.19763 bn, MG R$4.69719 bn, RJ R$3.87968 bn, RS R$2.55615 bn, BA R$1.711 bn, PE R$1.2444 bn, CE R$984.72 million. By 2002: 10 state banks privatised, 10 extinguished, 16 turned into development agencies, 5 stayed state-owned (counts from the ANPUH paper, not BNDES). State banks' share of financial-system assets fell from 17.6% (1996) to under 1.5%.
who_got: Itau and Bradesco were the most frequent buyers: Banerj (Itau, 26 Jun 1997), Credireal (BCN, 7 Aug 1997), Bemge (Itau, 14 Sep 1998), Bandepe (ABN Amro, 17 Nov 1998), Baneb (Bradesco, 22 Jun 1999), Paraiban (Real ABN Amro, 8 Nov 2001), BEG (Itau, 4 Dec 2001), BEA (Bradesco, 24 Jan 2002). Meridional (Bozano Simonsen, Dec 1997) was a federal-controlled bank, not a state bank in the PROES sense. Banco do Maranhao went to Bradesco in Feb 2004. Banespa and Banestado have their own cases.
terms: BCB table prices (R$ million): Banerj 311.10; Credireal 134.20; Bemge 603.06; Bandepe 182.90; Baneb 267.80; Banestado 1,799.26; Banespa 7,160.92; Paraiban 79.14; BEG 680.84; BEA 192.54; total R$11.41 bn including subsidiaries, employee sales and leftovers.
mechanism: MP 1.514/1996 and Lei 9.496/1997. Incentives: Banerj allowed part payment in privatization certificates; buyers could count the agio and Bemge's fixed assets toward the fixed-asset limit for five years; tax credits were the 'most controversial' incentive.
who_paid: Taxpayers. The Union's net debt is affected only by the interest differential. ANPUH puts the total PROES cost above R$73 bn, 'almost four times PROER', with about R$53 bn spent cleaning banks that were later privatised. Sul21 (opinion) puts debt assumption plus PROES at about R$500 bn in Dec-2010 prices, 90% to SP, RJ, MG and RS; the two numbers measure different things.
after: 49 administrative processes were opened and 10 denuncias sent to the Ministerio Publico (BCB book). BEM (2004) and BEC (2005) were sold later.
counter_view: Official BCB view: privatization was optional, but covering the uncovered liability was a legal obligation of the states, so comparing the federal loan with sale proceeds is 'simplistic'. The banks were already insolvent.

title: Companhia Vale do Rio Doce (6 May 1997)
what: 41.73% of voting shares of the world's top iron-ore company, with Carajas and large mineral rights (also described as 27% of total capital). The government kept 35.19% of ordinary shares (not confirmed).
who_got: Consorcio Brasil via Valepar (created 9 Apr 1997): CSN 16.30% (R$1.3 bn), Litel (Previ, Petros, Funcef, Fundacao Cesp) 10.43% (R$834.5 million), Eletron (Opportunity) 10% (R$800 million), Sweet River (NationsBank) 5% (R$400 million). One source says NationsBank put in R$1.2 bn, conflicting with R$400 million. Critics and one secondary article say BNDES gave subsidised financing; no official figure found.
terms: R$3.338 bn (about US$3.0 bn), a 19.99% premium over the R$26.67 minimum (R$32.00 per share). The company was valued at US$9.3 bn (R$10.4 bn) at the time (Merrill Lynch-led). Critics' ranges go to R$100 bn. Coppe-UFRJ: ore reserves reported to the US SEC in 1995 were Carajas 4.970 bn t and Sistema Sul 7.918 bn t, but the sale notice used 1.8 bn t and 1.4 bn t (gap 9.688 bn t); ore was valued in situ, not at the mine gate; excluded reserves valued at R$1.094 bn to R$87.579 bn depending on method; 104 deposits valued at zero were worth US$114.5 million. Titanium (92.5 Mt) and niobium (69.1 Mt) were not valued (DNPM document).
mechanism: PND auction (Lei 8.031) at the Rio stock exchange. Mining stayed under DNPM; no sector regulator.
who_paid: Brazil lost control of a strategic asset, say critics. Pension funds of state firms put in R$834.5 million (Litel). Six valuers were paid R$63.7 million.
after: Dozens of popular-action suits from 1997; in Oct 2005 TRF-1 sent 69 suits back to Belem for expert review; 107 suits counted in 2007 (Estadao via Wikipedia); in 2010 STF Justice Gilmar Mendes suspended annulment cases. A STJ ruling reported on 2 Sep 2024 (rapporteur Mauro Campbell, IAC 7) held that res judicata in one popular action binds all (erga omnes), applied the fait accompli doctrine and noted prior TCU approval; reported as ending 70+ suits. No re-nationalisation. Vale's market value was R$84.4 bn by March 2006 (market quote, not a valuation of what was sold).
counter_view: Roger Agnelli, then Vale's president: it was an open, public auction. The 2006 value is a later quote. The STJ found no damage and relied on TCU approval. The sale notice used two outside valuations plus a third review (BNDES pamphlet 'O Estado no lugar certo'). Unvalued mineral rights belong to the Union, not the company (defence line; not sourced in opened pages). A TCU document itself was not retrieved.

Federalised distributors (Ceal, Cepisa, Eletroacre, Ceron, Ceam) were taken into Eletrobras in 1997-99 and only privatised in 2018. Eletrobras also ran Enersul, Cemat, Saelpa, Cosern, Cemar and Celpa until their sales 1997-2000 (not checked).
who_got: Coelba (31 Jul 1997): Iberdrola 39%, Previ and Banco do Brasil 61%. CPFL (5 Nov 1997): VBC 46% and Previ 38%. Enersul (19 Nov 1997): Iven 52%. title: The 'grampo do BNDES' and the Tele Norte Leste/Telemar case
what: Tele Norte Leste went to the Telemar consortium for R$3.434 bn (TCU: R$3,434,000,108) in the 29 Jul 1998 auction. Recordings of officials discussing the consortium were revealed by Elio Gaspari in Folha de S.Paulo and O Globo on 8 Nov 1998.
who_got: Telemar (AG Telecom/Inepar, Andrade Gutierrez, Macal and others). The MPF alleged first-instalment funds came from BNDES, Banco do Brasil insurers and pension-fund-controlled firms, forming the consortium with 'illegal loans'. The defence says Previ was in the Opportunity consortium, not Telemar; the MPF argued Previ had a relevant role in Tele Norte Leste (disputed).
terms: BNDES help was R$686.8 million, 20% of the control price (TCU paragraph 266). The first instalment of R$1,373.6 million was paid with a R$400 million advance split between Andrade Gutierrez (133 million), Macal (133 million) and Inepar (134 million), then two further R$143.4 million tranches. A news site's 'almost half a billion reais' refers to the R$400 million first advance, not a conflict.
mechanism: BNDESPar financing; auction at the Rio exchange.
who_paid: TCU: BNDES made no studies proving the borrowers' (or guarantors') economic-financial capacity (paragraph 267). Dec 1998 determinations to BNDESPar: publicise financing in future sales, analyse borrowers' finances, and use a special auction when selling Telemar shares; three people were summoned to a hearing.
after: Luiz Carlos Mendonca de Barros testified in the Senate on 19 Nov 1998; he and Andre Lara Resende told Cardoso on 22 Nov 1998 they were leaving (Poder360). Wikipedia says four officials resigned (Mendonca de Barros, Lara Resende, Pio Borges, Jose Roberto Mendonca de Barros); only the first two are independently confirmed. The Federal Police declined to investigate (tapes illegally obtained) and the ruling parties blocked a CPI in May 1999 (Wikipedia only). In April 2010 the 3rd Turma of TRF-1, with Desembargador Tourinho Neto writing, rejected the MPF's improbity appeal; first instance (Judge Moacir Ferreira Ramos, 17a Vara DF) had already dismissed it.
counter_view: Defence outcome: TRF-1 relied on a TCU report that found no irregularity; the court said it is not bound by the TCU but a ruling aligned with it is not unreasoned, that annulment was 'not in the public interest', and that improbity needs bad faith. Defendants: Mendonca de Barros (ex-Communications Minister), Lara Resende (ex-BNDES president), Pio Borges (ex-interim BNDES president) and the former Anatel president. The FPA page says the tapes showed officials favouring Opportunity's bid, with no quotes; no confirmed transcript exists in the sources.

title: Electricity rationing and the tariff recomposition (RTE)
government: Cardoso (Camara de Gestao da Crise); settlement under Lula
what: Compulsory rationing from about Jun/Jul 2001 to Feb 2002 (one search result: 1 Jul 2001 to 19 Feb 2002). Targets: 20% for residential users above 100 kWh a month, 20% commercial, 20-25% industrial, with a surcharge for overshoot and a bonus for savers. The 2001 General Agreement (MP 14 of 21 Dec 2001, Lei 10.438 of 26 Apr 2002) set an Extraordinary Tariff Recomposition (RTE).
who_got: Distributors and generators, which lost revenue when use fell. Concessionaires' loss is put at R$8 bn by Pinguelli Rosa (one author; no official total in an opened page).
terms: RTE of 2.9% a year for residential (rural, public lighting) and 7.9% a year for others, none for low-income users; a news summary says it ran 72 months (snippet). The law also describes a one-time recomposition applied for 12 months. BNDES lent the firms the amount to be recomposed: about R$7 bn for RTE financing and R$8 bn for plants (TCU/BNDES reporting via Congresso em Foco).
mechanism: Contract rebalancing (reequilibrio economico-financeiro) by law, with BNDES credit.

An uncited blog saying about 60% was passed to consumers is unconfirmed.
after: Eight of 12 financed distributors had not settled their debts (Congresso em Foco). Many distributors had been privatised; they were barred from raising prices while sales fell, which created the liquidity crisis that the agreement moved to consumers and BNDES.
counter_view: Causes are disputed. The government and sector analysts blame a severe drought plus delays in generation works and missing long-term contracting rules. Critics blame low investment and a ban on Eletrobras investing because of privatization plans (FPA, a critical source). Castelar and Lessa argue rationing, not privatization, was the problem. The BNDES paper itself is the official view, not neutral.

title: Cedae (Rio de Janeiro) water and sewage concessions
government: Rio de Janeiro state government; BNDES designed the model
what: Water and sewage concession of the Rio metropolitan region in four blocks, auctioned 30 Apr 2021 on B3. Cedae stays as bulk water seller; about 30 municipalities stayed out.
who_got: Block 1: Aegea (R$8.2 bn). Block 2: Iguá (R$7.286 bn). Block 4: Aegea (R$7.2 bn). Block 3 had no winner and was re-auctioned to Aguas do Brasil for about R$2.2 bn (InvestNews snippet, unverified).
terms: R$22.7 bn total for three blocks against a R$10.6 bn minimum outorga. Block 1 minimum R$4.036 bn (agio 103.13%); Block 2 minimum R$3.172 bn (agio 129.68%); Block 4 agio about 188%. 35-year contracts, about R$30 bn of investment, about 13 million people.
mechanism: Concession auction. BNDES was structurer, not financier, as far as found.
who_paid: Not stated beyond tariff effects below.
after: Iguá owed a final outorga installment of R$1.8 bn due early Feb 2025, sought arbitration to deposit only R$828 million citing losses and social-tariff counts above the tender estimates, and the state regulator Agenersa denied suspension ('calote' is the outlet's word). In Oct 2025 a conciliation term cut the wholesale water cost by 24.13% over the sewage-coverage gap; Cedae withdrew in Dec 2025 and the TJ-RJ suspended the agreement. A 7.10% rebalancing increase was approved; the Feb 2026 adjustment was 9.75% (Block 1) and 8.09% (Block 4). Aguas do Rio serves about 10 million people in 27 municipalities. TCE-RJ suspension dates, and 10.97%/15.89% increases from Dec 2025 that conflict with the above, are unverified.
counter_view: Supporters read bids at more than twice the minimum as competition. Critics read them as a promise that tariffs or renegotiation would have to pay for it.

title: CEEE-D (Rio Grande do Sul), 2021
government: Rio Grande do Sul state government (Governor Leite)
what: The rump distributor left after the 1997 split, sold at an auction in 2021. Contract signed 8 Jul 2021.
who_got: Equatorial, the only bidder. CPFL did not bid, citing risk and return.
terms: R$100,000 (symbolic). Analysts assumed about R$3.5 bn of debt; ICMS debt alone exceeded R$3.3 bn. Equatorial must invest R$1.6 bn. The 2015 renewal to 2045 depended on quality indicators that CEEE-D missed two years running. Analysts put value at 1.5x-2x RAB.
mechanism: Share sale. No BNDES money found.
who_paid: The state shed the debt and the caducidade risk. Critics cite layoffs and outsourcing.
after: Equatorial serves about 1.7 million consumers in 72 municipalities. After the 16 Jan 2024 storm, Governor Leite threatened the concession. The Porto Alegre council opened a CPI. A May 2021 court suspension of the share sale (Sul21 snippet) and its outcome are unverified.
counter_view: Leite says private firms should deliver the service and the state could not fund the needed investment. The sale was needed to stop a caducidade risk (Brazil Journal).

title: Corsan (Rio Grande do Sul), 2022
government: Rio Grande do Sul state government (first state sanitation sale under the 2020 sanitation law)
what: B3 auction on 20 Dec 2022 of the state water company. Corsan served 307 municipalities and about 6 million people, with 5,995 employees and a R$943 million pension liability.
who_got: Aegea, sole bidder. Iguá, Aguas do Brasil and Equatorial visited but did not bid.
terms: R$4.151 bn, a 1.15% agio over the R$4.1 bn minimum. Aegea must invest R$12 bn to reach universal service by 2033. 198 of 317 municipalities had not signed regularization terms (38% of revenue). A union request to postpone was rejected by the TST.
mechanism: B3 auction under the 2020 sanitation law. No BNDES role found.
who_paid: Not stated.
after: Aegea took control in Jul 2023 with 5,600 employees; about 2,000 had left by Mar 2024; 18 months of job stability was agreed. Investment about R$2 bn a year against about R$500 million a year under the state. More than 200 contracts renegotiated. A TCE case seeks annulment. Tariff adjustments of 6.46% (Jan 2025) and 4.68% (Jan 2026), and a TJ-RS suspension of a 23.01% adjustment (undated), are unverified.
counter_view: Jerson Kelman: profit funds expansion (NeoFeed). The Sindiagua president (advocacy) says the TCE/RS rapporteur found the price underestimated and the 1a Camara recommended annulment.

title: Copel (Parana), 2023 share offering
what: Not a control sale. A share offering that cut the state's stake and created a company without a controller. Coordinators: BTG, Itau BBA, Bradesco BBI, UBS BB, Morgan Stanley.
who_got: Market investors. BNDES held 24% and did not buy.
terms: Base offer R$4.3 bn (R$4.95 bn with 15% greenshoe) at reference R$7.85. 41.9% primary. Parana's stake falls from 31.1% to 15.6%. Primary proceeds of R$1.9 bn fund a R$3.7 bn outorga for renewing Foz do Areia, Segredo and Salto Caxias (4.1 GW, 60% of capacity). A golden share was modelled on Eletrobras. Final numbers (unverified): R$5.2 bn (US$1.06 bn) raised and a 10% voting cap, from paywalled pages.
mechanism: Follow-on offering with a golden share.
who_paid: Not stated.
after: Not researched (too recent for tariff effects).
counter_view: Unions and some deputies said the state gave up control of water and power it used for industrial policy. Brazil Journal frames the state as keeping a veto through the golden share.
